title: The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations
engineering_principles: Defines a transaction as a state transformation with atomicity, durability and consistency; bad transactions are adjusted by further compensating transactions.
practical_examples: Contract and wedding-ceremony analogy for commit coordination.
why_it_matters: Origin of the correction-by-compensation model used by ledgers and sagas, and an early statement that very long transactions are an unsolved limitation.
authority_rationale: Foundational paper by a Turing Award recipient, presented at VLDB 1981.
notes: Tandem TR 81.3. The term ACID does not appear; isolation is not a named property.

title: Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery
organization_author: Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter (ACM Computing Surveys 15(4))
engineering_principles: Names the four ACID properties and defines a consistent database as one containing the results of successful transactions; incorrect committed work can only be removed by countertransactions.
practical_examples: Taxonomy of transaction, system and media failures with the recovery each requires.
why_it_matters: Shows that ACID consistency depends on correct transactions, so schemas should declare every invariant they can as constraints.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed survey that introduced the ACID acronym.
notes: University-hosted copy used because the ACM DL page (DOI 10.1145/289.291) returned HTTP 403.

title: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels
organization_author: Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil, O'Neil (Microsoft Research MSR-TR-95-51; ACM SIGMOD 1995)
engineering_principles: The ANSI phenomena are ambiguous and should be read broadly; dirty write must be excluded at every level; snapshot isolation is non-serializable and allows write skew.
practical_examples: Histories for each anomaly, including a bank constraint violated across two accounts.
why_it_matters: Supplies the vocabulary for stating which cross-row invariants each isolation level leaves exposed.
authority_rationale: Foundational peer-reviewed paper; authors include an ANSI SQL editor and Jim Gray.
notes: Text extracted locally. Table 4 is multi-line in extraction, so verify individual cells against the PDF before quoting them.

title: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL
organization_author: Dan R. K. Ports and Kevin Grittner (PVLDB 5(12))
engineering_principles: Serializability can be built on snapshots by aborting on two adjacent rw-antidependencies, so reads do not block; applications must be ready to retry.
practical_examples: Write-skew example and a three-transaction batch-processing anomaly involving a read-only report.
why_it_matters: Justifies PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE plus retry as a schema-independent way to protect cross-row invariants, at under 7% cost relative to SI in the reported benchmarks.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed VLDB paper by the implementers.
notes: Text extracted locally from the PDF.

title: PostgreSQL Documentation: 13.2 Transaction Isolation
engineering_principles: Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation; Serializable uses SSI; applications need a general retry mechanism for serialization failures and should keep transactions small.
practical_examples: Class-sum anomaly under Repeatable Read versus Serializable; DELETE ... WHERE hits = 10 race under Read Committed.
why_it_matters: Normative source for PostgreSQL guarantees and the retry contract.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: PostgreSQL 18.6 documentation at time of access.

title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Transaction Isolation Levels
engineering_principles: Plain SELECTs use a read view while locking statements see the latest committed state, so mixing them in one REPEATABLE READ transaction is discouraged.
practical_examples: Two-session UPDATE examples comparing lock retention under REPEATABLE READ and READ COMMITTED.
why_it_matters: Explains why read-then-write logic on MySQL needs locking reads or SERIALIZABLE, and how index design determines which rows lock.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Read alongside TXN-11, which reports weaker behavior than the level name suggests.

title: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL (Transact-SQL)
engineering_principles: READ COMMITTED is lock-based on SQL Server unless RCSI is enabled, while RCSI is the default on Azure SQL Database; isolation level does not change exclusive locks taken for writes.
practical_examples: Session-level SET statement with REPEATABLE READ; READCOMMITTEDLOCK hint under RCSI.
why_it_matters: Guarantees depend on database options as well as level name, so a framework must record both.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: publication_date is ms.date; page updated_at is 2026-11-02. Azure Synapse defaults to READ UNCOMMITTED.

title: Oracle Database Concepts: Data Concurrency and Consistency
engineering_principles: Readers and writers do not block each other; a serializable transaction fails when updating a row changed by a transaction that committed after it began.
practical_examples: ORA-08177 handling options: commit work so far, roll back to a savepoint, or roll back the transaction.
why_it_matters: Oracle SERIALIZABLE does not protect against write skew according to TXN-10, so cross-row invariants need explicit locks or constraints.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: URL path is release 23 but the served content identifies as Oracle AI Database 26. The page does not mention write skew.

title: MongoDB Manual: Transactions
engineering_principles: Snapshot guarantees hold only when the transaction commits with w: majority; transactions should not replace good schema design.
practical_examples: Embedding related data to avoid multi-document transactions.
why_it_matters: Makes the aggregate-as-document choice a correctness decision and requires concerns to be set explicitly.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Runtime limits and write-conflict behavior are on the separate Production Considerations page.

title: Hermitage: Testing transaction isolation levels
engineering_principles: Isolation level names are not portable; guarantees must be established per engine by testing specific anomalies.
practical_examples: Scripted concurrent session tests per anomaly across PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, CockroachDB and YugabyteDB.
why_it_matters: Provides the empirical basis for an engine-by-level anomaly matrix.
authority_rationale: Reproducible test suite by a recognized distributed-systems researcher; not peer-reviewed.
notes: Engine versions and last-updated date are not stated. The MySQL MAV classification is disputed by TXN-11. Title is descriptive of the repository.

title: Jepsen: MySQL 8.0.34
organization_author: Peter Alvaro and Kyle Kingsbury, Jepsen
engineering_principles: MySQL Repeatable Read transactions cannot safely read a value and then write it; use Serializable or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
practical_examples: Single-node histories with values changing inside one transaction; RDS Multi-AZ anomalies tied to replica commit ordering.
why_it_matters: Shows the default level of a widely used ERP backend needs explicit locking or version checks for read-modify-write.
authority_rationale: Widely recognized independent testing with published histories.
notes: Tested 8.0.34; re-check against 8.4 before relying on it for that release.

title: Jepsen: PostgreSQL 12.3
engineering_principles: Even a mature serializable implementation can have bugs, so guarantees should be tested and engines kept patched.
practical_examples: G2-item under serializable caused by conflict detection crediting the wrong transaction ID.
why_it_matters: Confirms Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation and sets a minimum patch expectation for SERIALIZABLE-based designs.
authority_rationale: Widely recognized independent testing; the defect was confirmed by a PostgreSQL developer.
notes: The report describes a patch scheduled for the 2020-08-13 minor release.

title: Jepsen: Consistency Models
engineering_principles: Snapshot isolation and repeatable read are incomparable; snapshot isolation, cursor stability, sequential and anything stronger are unavailable in asynchronous networks.
practical_examples: Implication map across multi-object and single-object models.
why_it_matters: Lets a framework state what a chosen model costs in availability.
authority_rationale: Widely used practitioner reference grounded in the formal literature.

title: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design: CAP is Only Part of the Story
engineering_principles: CAP limits behavior only during failures; the latency-consistency tradeoff shapes normal operation.
practical_examples: Classifies Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak as PA/EL; VoltDB/H-Store and Megastore as PC/EC; MongoDB as PA/EC; PNUTS as PC/EL.
why_it_matters: Separates system-of-record choices (PC/EC) from latency-favoring read replicas for analytics.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed magazine article by a leading database researcher that introduced PACELC.
notes: System classifications reflect 2012 defaults and are dated, notably MongoDB. The full PACELC sentence quoted in the notes should be checked against the PDF because extraction was reviewed in a truncated column.

title: CAP Twelve Years Later: How the "Rules" Have Changed
organization_author: Eric Brewer (IEEE Computer; republished by InfoQ)
engineering_principles: CAP prohibits only perfect availability and consistency during partitions; detect partitions, limit operations, then recover and compensate.
practical_examples: ATM preserving balance >= 0 by capping withdrawals during a partition and fixing violations afterward.
why_it_matters: Shows how to design bounded degraded-mode operations and post-partition audit trails.
authority_rationale: Written by the originator of the CAP conjecture and published by IEEE Computer.
notes: publication_date is the InfoQ republication date; the original appeared in IEEE Computer, February 2012.

title: A Critique of the CAP Theorem
engineering_principles: CAP's definitions are inconsistent and ambiguous; reason about how operation latency responds to network delay.
practical_examples: Delay-sensitivity framework for comparing consistency guarantees.
why_it_matters: Warns against selecting a database from a CP or AP label alone.
authority_rationale: Preprint by a recognized researcher; not peer-reviewed.
notes: Only the abstract page was read, not the full paper.

title: Sagas
organization_author: Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem (ACM SIGMOD 1987)
engineering_principles: A long-lived transaction can be a sequence of interleavable transactions that all complete or are amended by compensating transactions.
practical_examples: Airline reservation split into per-seat transactions; bank statements and insurance claims as long-lived transactions.
why_it_matters: Basis for saga state tables and the requirement that each step has a defined compensation.
authority_rationale: Foundational peer-reviewed paper.
notes: Cornell copy used because the ACM DL page returned HTTP 403. OCR quality is poor, so check quotes against the scan.

title: Pattern: Transactional outbox
engineering_principles: Store messages in the same local transaction as business changes and relay them separately; consumers must tolerate duplicates.
practical_examples: Relay implemented by polling publisher or transaction log tailing.
why_it_matters: Requires an outbox table and consumer de-duplication in place of 2PC.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner pattern catalog by the author of Microservices Patterns.
notes: The page does not specify outbox columns.

title: Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres
engineering_principles: Group local work into atomic phases between external calls, record a recovery point, and enforce one key per user with a unique index.
practical_examples: Table with user_id, idempotency_key, locked_at, request_params, response_code, response_body and recovery_point, using SERIALIZABLE phases that map conflicts to 409.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete table shape for safe API retries in financial and SaaS systems.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner with payments-API experience; not official Stripe documentation.
notes: The retention horizon is stated as about 24 hours in one place and about 72 hours in another.

title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
engineering_principles: Exposing clock uncertainty enables external consistency; the authors prefer that programmers handle overuse of transactions rather than code around their absence.
practical_examples: Commit wait until TT.after(s); two-phase commit run over Paxos groups.
why_it_matters: Counterweight to the claim that 2PC is never viable, relevant when choosing a geo-distributed system of record.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed systems paper from the system's builders.
notes: Detailed claims in the notes come from the linked PDF, which is the ACM TOCS 31(3) 2013 version rather than the OSDI text.
